notes.b: A family passes through a sequence of stages, and at each one its priorities, income and time change. Managing well means adjusting to the stage the family is in, because the same family needs different things as its members age.
points: The stages include a newly married couple, a family with young children, a family with school-going children, a family with teenagers and an older couple whose children have left home.
Young children need constant care, time, money and space for feeding and supervision, so childcare and daily routines become central to management, and free time is limited.
A parent who works fewer hours to care for young children often brings in a reduced income, which makes money tighter just as costs rise.
School-going children and teenagers raise costs for clothing, books, school costs, leisure and activities, and teenagers also need planning for further education.
Older children can take on tasks and join family decisions, which reduces the workload on parents. In short, as children get older they become part of the decision-making process.
Newly married couples and childless households often have more freedom, more flexible time and more income for leisure than families with young children.
Older people may have a reduced income after retirement and reduced mobility, or greater health needs, which affects choices about food, transport and housing.
Priorities differ for a family with children and a family without, because children add costs, tasks and decisions that a couple alone does not face.
notes.tip: Exams ask how stage in the life cycle affects management. Give a stage and its effect: young children need time, money and space, while older children help and join decisions.

notes.b: Employment pattern means the number of family members working, whether inside or outside the home, the type of job and the hours worked. It matters because it decides how much money there is to manage and when family members are free to carry out tasks.
points: A dual-income household (two earners) has more money available but less time for housework and meal preparation.
A single-income household has less money to manage, so budgeting and prioritising essentials are more critical.
Full-time, part-time, job-sharing, flexible and seasonal hours each change when family members are available for tasks, so household work must be fitted around them.
Shift work and night work change meal times and sleep patterns, so family routines must be built around the shifts.
Commuting (the daily journey to work) uses time and money, which affects the family budget and the time left for household work.
Working from home, or a parent working abroad, changes how tasks and childcare are shared between family members.
notes.tip: Keep employment pattern (hours and type of work, and their effect on money and time) separate from sex roles (who is expected to do tasks). Explain each on its own and give an example, such as how shift work affects meal times.

notes.b: A dual role means carrying two demands at once. This puts pressure on time and energy, so families need ways of managing it.
points: A dual role arises when both partners work outside the home, so extra planning is needed for childcare, meals and housework.
A lone-parent household has the extra demand of being both earner and parent, with no second adult to share tasks and decisions.
Sharing and delegating tasks spreads the workload, so no one person is overloaded.
Making a weekly plan or list, such as a weekly planning meeting or a shared calendar, helps the household stay organised and avoid missed tasks.
Using childcare and time-saving equipment frees time that would otherwise go on routine tasks.
Communicating regularly lets family members raise problems early and adjust the plan.
notes.tip: Dual role means both partners in paid work, or a lone parent combining earner and carer. Do not assign it to one sex. Short questions can ask how being a lone-parent household affects management.

notes.b: Culture and values both shape the decisions a family makes. Culture is what a group shares, while values are what the family itself believes matters most.
points: Culture is the shared customs, beliefs and way of life of a group. It affects family management through dress code, the food a family eats, religious practices, and festivals and celebrations.
Culture also shapes expectations of roles, such as who earns income, who cooks, and who cares for children and older relatives.
Culture can affect spending and the use of time, for example around religious festivals and family traditions, when money and time are set aside for them.
Values are a family's beliefs about what is important, such as health, education, family time, faith, sustainability, community or security.
Values determine the decisions a family takes, such as buying local food, choosing organic produce, reducing waste, how much to save, and how money and time are shared.
Values can change when circumstances change, for example after the illness of a family member, so the decisions that follow from them change too.
notes.tip: If asked how values, culture or standards affect management, pair the factor with its effect and one example, such as buying organic food for values or festival spending for culture. A list of names alone earns few marks.

notes.b: Standards are the quality a family expects of itself, and sex roles are what is expected of each partner. Both decide how much work there is and who does it.
points: Standards are the level of quality a family sets for its home, meals, appearance and finances, such as how clean the house is kept or how meals are presented.
Standards decide how much time, money and energy a task takes, because a higher standard means more effort.
High standards can cause strain and overload in a family short of time or money; very low standards can affect health and comfort.
Standards can be reviewed and adjusted when circumstances change, for example lowering a housework standard when time becomes short.
Sex roles (also called gender roles in papers) are the roles and behaviour expected of men and women in the household.

Traditionally men were the earners and women did most household work and caring. Roles are now increasingly equal, with partners sharing earning, childcare, cooking and cleaning, and tasks assigned on fairness rather than sex. Rotating tasks is one way to do this.
Sharing roles reduces overload and gives more equal decision-making. When one partner is expected to carry all household tasks, the workload becomes unfair and management is more strained.
notes.tip: Use the syllabus term sex roles and note that gender roles means the same thing in papers. Exams ask how roles that are more equal, with tasks shared, affect a family managing the home.

notes.h: Lifestyle: socio-economic status and family composition
notes.b: Lifestyle is the way a family lives: its pattern of work, leisure, eating, spending and travel. The syllabus ties it to socio-economic status and family composition, because these shape the resources and needs a family has.
points: Socio-economic status is a family's position in society, based on income, occupation and education. Socio-economic status affects income, which sets the total resources available to the family and the choices it can make.
Families from lower socio-economic backgrounds tend to emphasise needs such as food, heating and housing, because income is limited.
Families from higher socio-economic backgrounds tend to have more scope for wants, luxuries, leisure and extra services.
Socio-economic group also influences educational opportunity and the type of job available, and so future income.

Family composition is the number of people in the family, the presence of members with special needs, such as a family member with a disability or an older relative needing care, and whether it is a one-parent or two-parent family.
A larger family needs more food, clothing, space and money, so budgets and meal plans must be scaled up.
A family member with a disability or special needs may raise household costs and reduce the time or ability of others to earn.
A lone parent has one income and one adult for all tasks, so management is more demanding.
notes.tip: Say that families on lower incomes tend to emphasise needs and families on higher incomes tend to emphasise luxuries, rather than stating it as a rule. Composition, life-cycle stage, employment patterns and socio-economic status have the clearest effects, so choose these when asked to discuss four factors, and give an effect and an example for each.

keyTerms.definition: The sequence of stages a family passes through over time, each with different priorities and resource needs.
The way family members work, including the number of earners, hours worked and where the work takes place.
The situation where a family member must combine paid work outside the home with the responsibilities of a parent or home manager.
The shared customs, food, dress, religious practices and celebrations that shape how a family lives and manages its home.
A family's beliefs about what matters most, which guide its decisions.
The levels of quality a family sets for its home, meals, appearance and finances.
The behaviour and responsibilities expected of men and women within a household.
A family's position based on its income, occupation and education, which affects the resources it has.
The number and make-up of the people in a family, including children and members with special needs.
The everyday pattern of work, leisure, eating and travel that a family follows.

factCards.term: Five typical stages of the family life cycle
factCards.definition: Newly married couple; family with young children; family with school-going children; family with teenagers; older couple after the children have left home.

factCards.term: Three effects of young children on family management
factCards.definition: Their needs for time, money and space increase; childcare and routines must be planned; daily timetables and budgets are built around their care.

factCards.term: Three effects of shift work on household management
factCards.definition: Meal times change; sleep patterns change; routines must be built around the shift pattern.

factCards.term: Four ways culture can affect family management
factCards.definition: Dress code; the food eaten; religious practices; festivals and celebrations.

factCards.term: Three ways a family's values can change how it is managed
factCards.definition: Choosing local shopping; choosing organic or sustainable food; changing priorities when circumstances change, such as illness.
Number of people in the family; presence of members with special needs; number of children; whether it is a lone-parent or two-parent household.

factCards.term: Two ways a dual-income household differs from a single-income household
factCards.definition: It has more money for spending, saving and credit repayments; it has less time for household tasks.

questions.prompt: Explain how a family's stage in the life cycle affects the management of its home. Give two examples.
questions.model: Two points at 3 marks each. Young children need time, money and space for care, so childcare and daily routines must be planned around them. Teenagers increase spending on clothing, books and school costs and need planning for further education; older children can take on tasks and join family decisions, reducing the parents' workload. Any two well-explained examples with a clear link to management earn full marks.

questions.prompt: Discuss how employment patterns and culture affect the management of a family's resources. Use examples from family life in your answer.
questions.model: Employment patterns: a dual-income household has more money but less time, so planning, delegation and shared tasks are needed; a single-income household has less money, so budgeting for essentials is critical. Shift work changes meal times and sleep patterns, so routines are built around the shift pattern. Commuting adds time and cost to the budget. Culture: food, dress code, religious practices and festivals shape spending and the timing of tasks; culture also shapes expectations of who does which tasks and who earns income. Link: a family that works shifts and follows a religious festival calendar must plan its meals, budget and time around both, combining the influence of employment and culture on its resource management.
